lessons.title: From Bretton Woods to the WTO Era: The Arc of Trade Liberalization

children.text: In March 2018, a fund manager watching an export-heavy basket on the BSE saw the Nifty Metal index fall nearly 3% in a single session. No Indian company had missed earnings. No domestic policy had changed. Washington had announced steel and aluminium tariffs under Section 232, on the other side of the planet, and the shock still moved Dalal Street. Three decades earlier, a tariff spat between two other countries would barely have registered on an Indian trading floor. India's economy was largely closed, global trade rules were thin, and capital moved slowly across borders. That transmission mechanism exists today because of a deliberate, decades-long project: the postwar effort to build a rules-based system for global trade. To understand why that system is now under visible strain, you first need to understand how it was built.

body.text: Global trade liberalization was not something that happened to the world. It was built, treaty by treaty, over eight decades, and every stage of that build now shapes how a tariff announcement in Washington moves a metal stock on the BSE.

children.text: 1944: Bretton Woods and the Architecture of Managed Trade

Delegates from 44 Allied nations met at a hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July 1944, determined not to repeat the 1930s: competitive currency devaluations, spiralling tariffs, and a collapse in world trade that deepened the Great Depression. The conference produced two institutions that still shape markets today, the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank, along with a system of fixed exchange rates in which currencies were pegged to the US dollar, and the dollar itself was pegged to gold at $35 an ounce.

A third institution was planned alongside them: an International Trade Organization, meant to set global rules for trade the way the IMF set rules for currencies. The US Congress never ratified it. In its place, a stopgap survived and eventually outgrew its designers' intentions.

body.label: Bretton Woods Conference
body.context: 44 Allied nations met in New Hampshire and created the IMF and the World Bank, and fixed the dollar to gold at $35 an ounce.

children.text: 1947: GATT Fills the Gap

The General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade was signed in October 1947 by 23 founding contracting parties, India among them. GATT was never meant to be a permanent institution, it was a provisional treaty. But it survived for nearly half a century because it worked, run through a series of negotiating
rounds
where member countries traded tariff cuts against each other.

markDefs.definition: A rule requiring a country to extend the same favourable trade terms, such as a tariff cut, to every other member it applies to any one member. It is the core non-discrimination principle of the GATT/WTO system.

children.text: GATT's core rule was
most-favoured-nation treatment

: a tariff cut given to one member had to be given to all members. This single rule is why a bilateral negotiation between, say, the US and Japan could ratchet down tariffs for the entire trading system at once.

cells: First round, 45,000 tariff concessions among 23 founding members
First round to negotiate across-the-board tariff cuts instead of product by product
Cut average tariffs on manufactured goods further and addressed non-tariff barriers for the first time
Created the WTO, extended rules to services and intellectual property, added binding dispute settlement

children.text: 1971: The Nixon Shock Ends Fixed Exchange Rates

The Bretton Woods currency system depended on the US holding enough gold to back every dollar held abroad. By the late 1960s, war spending and rising imports had made that promise impossible to keep. On 15 August 1971, President Richard Nixon suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, a move markets remember as the Nixon Shock. Fixed exchange rates limped on for another two years under a patched agreement, then collapsed. By 1973, the major currencies were floating against each other, and currency movement became a permanent, independent variable in trade competitiveness, on top of tariffs.

columns.label: Bretton Woods system (1944-1971)
points: Currencies pegged to the dollar, dollar pegged to gold
Exchange rate risk mostly managed by governments
Trade competitiveness set mainly by tariffs and productivity
Capital controls were common and expected

columns.label: Floating rate era (1971 onward)
points: Currencies float, priced by markets in real time
Exchange rate risk shifts onto exporters, importers and investors
Trade competitiveness set by tariffs, productivity and currency moves together
Capital gradually liberalized across most large economies

children.text: 1991: India Opens Up, in Step With the World

India's own opening was not a coincidence of timing. By June 1991, India's foreign exchange reserves had fallen to roughly $1.2 billion, barely enough to cover a few weeks of imports, forcing the government to airlift gold reserves to the Bank of England and the Union Bank of Switzerland as collateral for emergency loans. Prime Minister P V Narasimha Rao and Finance Minister Manmohan Singh used the crisis to push through reforms that had been debated for years: industrial delicensing, a two-step devaluation of the rupee of roughly 18 to 19%, and the start of sustained FDI liberalization.

body.text: India's 1991 reforms were part of a much wider wave. China had already begun opening its economy in 1978 under Deng Xiaoping. Much of Latin America liberalized trade through the 1980s and early 1990s. Vietnam launched its own Doi Moi reforms in 1986. India joined a global current that was already running, which is one reason its opening coincided almost exactly with the final years of the Uruguay Round.

children.text: 1995: GATT Becomes the WTO

The Uruguay Round, launched in 1986 and concluded in 1994 at Marrakesh, did what the failed International Trade Organization could not. It created the World Trade Organization, which came into force on 1 January 1995 with roughly 123 founding members, India among them as a founding member rather than a later joiner. Three changes mattered most for how trade actually works today.
Binding dispute settlement.
Under GATT, a losing party could block a ruling against it. Under the WTO, rulings apply automatically unless every member, including the winner, votes to block them, which almost never happens.
Services and intellectual property, covered for the first time.
The General Agreement on Trade in Services and the TRIPS agreement on intellectual property extended the rulebook far beyond physical goods.
Tariffs, cut to historic lows.
Average tariffs on industrial goods among developed economies fell from roughly 40% when GATT began in 1947 to roughly 4% by the time the Uruguay Round closed.

stats.label: WTO founding members, 1995
stats.context: India joined as a founding member, not a later accession

stats.label: Developed-economy industrial tariffs, 1947 to mid-1990s

children.text: 2001: China Joins the WTO, and Hyperglobalization Begins

markDefs.definition: A term used by economists including Dani Rodrik for the sharp acceleration in global trade integration roughly from the early 2000s to the 2008 financial crisis, driven above all by China's entry into the WTO and the offshoring of manufacturing it enabled.

children.text: China's accession to the WTO on 11 December 2001, after 15 years of negotiation, is widely treated as the single event that opened the era economists call
hyperglobalization

. Binding China's low labour costs and manufacturing scale to WTO rules gave multinational companies the legal certainty to offshore production there at a pace that would have been too risky before. Global merchandise trade, and world trade as a share of world GDP, both accelerated sharply through the following seven years.

body.title: The Arc of Trade Liberalization, 1944 to 2001

events.title: Bretton Woods Conference
events.description: IMF and World Bank created; dollar pegged to gold, other currencies pegged to the dollar.

events.title: GATT signed
events.description: 23 founding members, including India, begin rounds of reciprocal tariff cuts.

events.title: Nixon Shock
events.description: Dollar-gold convertibility suspended; fixed exchange rates collapse by 1973.

events.title: India's economic reforms begin
events.description: Balance of payments crisis forces delicensing, rupee devaluation and FDI liberalization.

events.title: WTO founded
events.description: Uruguay Round concludes; binding dispute settlement, services and IP rules added.

events.title: China joins the WTO
events.description: Widely marked as the start of the hyperglobalization era that ran through 2008.

body.title: Test the arc
body.question: Which event is most directly responsible for ending the fixed exchange rate system that Bretton Woods had built?
options: The founding of the WTO in 1995
body.explanation: The Nixon Shock suspended the dollar's convertibility into gold, the anchor the entire fixed-rate system depended on. Fixed rates staggered on briefly under the Smithsonian Agreement, then gave way to floating currencies by 1973.

body.title: Apply the WTO's dispute mechanism
body.scenario: In the mid-2010s, a wave of low-priced solar cell and module imports from China put pressure on Indian manufacturers. India eventually imposed anti-dumping and safeguard duties on these imports, actions that were themselves challenged at the WTO by trading partners over India's domestic content requirements for solar procurement.
body.prompt: Explain, in your own words, why this entire episode, both India's ability to impose duties and other countries' ability to challenge India's domestic content rules, could only unfold the way it did because of the institutional changes made in 1995. What would have been different under the old GATT system?
body.modelAnswer: Under GATT, dispute rulings could be blocked by the losing party, so a ruling against India's domestic content requirements, or against duties India imposed, could simply have been vetoed and left unresolved. The WTO's binding dispute settlement, introduced in 1995, meant panel rulings applied automatically. That is what gave both sides, India defending its solar manufacturing policy and its trading partners challenging it, a predictable legal process to fight the dispute through, rather than a purely diplomatic or political stand-off outside any rulebook.

body.title: The Arc of Trade Liberalization: Core Terms

cards.definition: The 1944 to 1971 framework of fixed exchange rates pegged to a gold-backed dollar, alongside the founding of the IMF and World Bank.
General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade, signed 1947, the provisional treaty that governed world trade through successive negotiating rounds until the WTO replaced it in 1995.
The rule that a trade concession given to one WTO member must be extended to all members, the core non-discrimination principle of the system.
The August 1971 suspension of dollar-gold convertibility that effectively ended the Bretton Woods fixed exchange rate system.
The 1986 to 1994 GATT negotiating round that created the WTO and extended trade rules to services and intellectual property.
The sharp acceleration in global trade integration from roughly 2001 to 2008, driven above all by China's WTO accession.

points: The postwar trade system was built deliberately, starting with the 1944 Bretton Woods conference and the institutions it created.
GATT, signed in 1947 as a stopgap after the International Trade Organization failed to be ratified, ran the system for nearly five decades through successive tariff-cutting rounds.
The 1971 Nixon Shock ended fixed exchange rates, adding currency movement as a permanent variable in trade competitiveness alongside tariffs.
India's 1991 reforms, forced by a balance of payments crisis, were part of a global wave of liberalization that included China from 1978 and much of Latin America through the 1980s.
The WTO, founded in 1995, added binding dispute settlement and extended rules to services and intellectual property, tools still actively used in disputes involving India today.

China's WTO accession in December 2001 is widely marked as the start of hyperglobalization, the sharp acceleration in trade integration that the next lesson picks up, along with the shocks that eventually broke it.
